items.stem: Before you try it: two sessions both read slots = 1, with no transaction. Both pass the check and both write. How many enrollments exist at the end?

options.text: Two, so the seat is sold twice.
options.feedback: Both sessions read 1 before either one wrote, so both believed a seat was free.

options.text: One, because the database stops the second session.
options.feedback: Nothing stops the second session. The database does not know that the two sessions are competing for the same seat.

options.text: One, because the second UPDATE fails when slots is already 0.
options.feedback: The UPDATE sets slots to 0 whatever the current value is, so it does not fail.

options.text: Zero, because the two sessions cancel each other.
options.feedback: Neither session is undone. Both insert an enrollment.

items.try: Open the "No transaction" tab in the widget above, press Run it, and read the Seats left column and the final result.

items.stem: A developer wraps the same statements in BEGIN and COMMIT and expects the problem to disappear. What happens?

options.text: Both sessions can still read 1 and both enroll, so the seat sells twice.
options.feedback: A transaction groups statements into one unit, but at the default isolation level it does not lock the row.

options.text: The database stops the second session from enrolling.
options.feedback: Nothing checks the earlier read. Both sessions already read 1 before either wrote, so both go ahead. Holding the row for the whole decision needs SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.

options.text: The database rolls back the second enrollment automatically.
options.feedback: The database rolls back only on an error. Nothing is wrong with the second session's statements.

options.text: Only one session can run BEGIN at a time on the same table.
options.feedback: Many sessions can have transactions open at once.

items.stem: Which fix lets the second student find out that the seat is gone, without a separate lock?

options.text: One `UPDATE ... WHERE slots > 0`, then check the rows changed.
options.feedback: The check and the change happen in one statement, so there is no gap, and a row count of 0 tells the second student that the seat is gone.

options.text: Lock the row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` before deciding.
options.feedback: This also works, but it locks the row and the second session waits for the first to finish. The question asks for a fix without a separate lock.

options.text: Read the seat count twice before writing the new value.
options.feedback: A second read still leaves a gap between reading and writing. Another session can write in that gap.

options.text: Add more web servers so each session has its own copy.
options.feedback: More web servers add more sessions that read the same row. The seat is contested in the database.

items.stem: A COMMIT returns successfully and then the server loses power. After the restart, the enrollment is still in the table. Which guarantee made that happen?

options.feedback: Durability means a committed change has been written to disk and survives a power failure.
Atomicity means all of a transaction's statements happen or none do. It does not cover power failures after the commit.
Consistency means declared rules stay true. It does not decide whether a change survives a restart.
Isolation controls what sessions see of each other's work while they run. It has nothing to do with restarts.
